question: Before farming, how did people get, cook and burn fat — and what do the oldest traces of it show?
summary: For most of human history fat was animal fat, and getting it took work. At Neumark-Nord in central Germany, Neanderthals about 125,000 years ago crushed the bones of at least 172 large mammals and heated them in water to render grease ([[te1]]). The recorded practice of northern hunters, who crack bones for marrow, boil the fragments and mix marrow and back-fat into akutuk and pemmican, shows what such an economy looked like ([[ec2]]); and hunters chose the fattest animals, Aleut sea lions and bison among them, which may have helped make domestication attractive ([[th1]]).

Fat was also light and part of cooking. Stone lamps in Lascaux and other Upper Palaeolithic caves burned animal fat ([[te2]]), and in Japan the earliest pots, of 15,000 to 11,800 years ago, were used to cook freshwater and marine animals ([[ec1]]), so marine fat is in the story from the start. Plant oil is barely present: only heaps of wild olive stones that were gathered, not pressed ([[ec3]]).
The folio is short because the evidence is archaeological and mostly reached here as press reports and abstracts. Its point is that fat was a human need long before any crop was pressed.

themes.title: Grease from bones
text: Crushing and boiling bones for grease is a Neanderthal practice at Neumark-Nord and the recorded method of northern hunters, who prize marrow for its oleic acid.

themes.title: Fat for light and for the pot
text: Lamps that burn animal fat, and the first pots, in which aquatic foods are cooked.

themes.title: Choosing the fattest
text: Hunters select the fattest animals; wild olives are gathered; the pull of fat may have shaped domestication.

turning_points.text: Neanderthals render bone grease at Neumark-Nord.
Stone lamps burn animal fat in the caves of the Upper Palaeolithic.
Jōmon pots cook fish and sea animals.

how_to_read: Six entries, so read straight through. Dates are very approximate; three are placeholders for the end of the Ice Age or for a range given as ‘Palaeolithic and Neolithic’. The *picture by region* shows how few places the evidence comes from.
The next folio starts at 8000 BC with the first butter and the first crops pressed for oil.

sources.intro: Almost all of this folio rests on web summaries of recent archaeological papers (Neumark-Nord, Lascaux, the Jōmon pots), on Kiple’s chapters on northern hunters, and on one line in a popular history of olive oil.
main: Press coverage of Kindler et al. 2025 ([[te1]]); the French Ministry of Culture’s Lascaux page and a 2002 article ([[te2]]); Craig et al. 2013 as abstracted ([[ec1]]).
Kiple for marrow, pemmican and the choice of fat animals ([[ec2]], [[th1]]); Mueller for the wild olive ([[ec3]]).
contested: The Neumark-Nord ‘fat factory’ is the press’s framing of one paper ([[te1]]); the start of fat lamps at 40,000 years comes from a hobbyist page ([[te2]]).
The marrow and fat-selection entries are CONTEXT: they use recorded practice and an argument, not Palaeolithic finds ([[ec2]], [[th1]]).
gaps: Africa, where our species began, has no entry: the sources found concern Europe, Japan and North America, and nothing in the library covers African Stone Age fats. Work such as John Speth’s studies of bone grease would help.
Marine fats elsewhere — the Arctic, the Pacific coasts, the Indian Ocean fish-eaters — and the Near East before farming are not covered; nor are plant fats such as nuts, which leave little trace.

text: The two European sites: the bone-grease works at Neumark-Nord and the fat lamps of Lascaux and other caves ([[te1]], [[te2]]).
No entry. The Near East’s fat story begins in the next folio, with the first butter.
One entry: the Jōmon pots of Japan, cooking freshwater and marine animals ([[ec1]]).
No entry, the biggest hole in the folio: the sources found and the library hold nothing on African Stone Age fats, though the continent is where our species began.
Two entries from recorded northern practice, not Palaeolithic finds: marrow, bone juice and pemmican, and the Aleut and bison hunters’ choice of the fattest animals ([[ec2]], [[th1]]).
The wild olive stones of the Mediterranean basin, a range spanning three continents ([[ec3]]).
